metadata.source: American Psychological Association, SAMHSA, Mayo Clinic, CDC, Gottman Institute, Parent-Child Interaction Therapy (PCIT), Evidence-based parenting research
metadata.description: Evidence-based guidance for parents supporting youth mental health
metadata.note: Created for parents co-using this dashboard with their teens

content.overview: Adolescent mental health challenges are more common than you think. Understanding what's normal teenage emotion vs. concerning patterns helps you respond effectively without overreacting or dismissing real struggles.
stats: 1 in 5 youth experience mental illness each year
70% of youth don't seek help (especially boys)
Family involvement increases treatment success by 20-30%

depression.normal: Sad mood for a few days after stress/disappointment; wanting alone time sometimes
depression.concerning: Persistent low mood 2+ weeks; loss of interest in everything; changes in sleep/appetite; inability to focus; thoughts of worthlessness

anxiety.normal: Nervousness about tests, social situations, or new experiences; temporary worry
anxiety.concerning: Constant worry interfering with daily life; physical symptoms (panic, racing heart) without cause; avoidance limiting activities; difficulty concentrating

self_harm.normal: Not normal; any self-harm signals distress and need for intervention
self_harm.concerning: Cutting, burning, hitting self; scratching until bleeding; hair pulling (trichotillomania); escalating pattern

social_changes.normal: Preferring peers over family sometimes; changing friend groups; experimenting with identity
social_changes.concerning: Complete social withdrawal; losing all friends; dramatic personality shift; engaging with harmful groups; sudden behavioral changes

content.brain_development_context: Your teen's brain is still developing (especially the prefrontal cortex responsible for impulse control and emotional regulation). This is why teens seem emotionally intense, impulsive, or dramatic - it's neurobiology, not character flaw. Understanding this helps you stay calm and supportive rather than dismissive.

subsections.title: The Teen Brain
subsections.content: Ages 13-19: Rapid brain reorganization. Emotions are more intense. Decision-making is impulsive. Sleep patterns shift (natural bedtime moves later). Risk tolerance increases. This is NORMAL and temporary.

subsections.title: Risk Factors to Watch
subsections.content: Social media comparison, perfectionism, academic pressure, peer stress, family conflict, trauma history, sleep deprivation, social isolation. Any of these + genetic predisposition can trigger mental health challenges.

sections.title: How to Talk About Mental Health

content.overview: Most parents don't know how to start the conversation. Here's the evidence-based approach (Emotion Coaching framework from Gottman Institute).

step1.name: Awareness: Notice emotional cues
step1.description: Your teen looks withdrawn, snapping at everyone, or seemed upset. Don't ignore it, but also don't ambush them.
tips: Wait for a calm moment (car rides, walks are better than dinnertime)
Notice physical changes (sleep, appetite, energy, hygiene)

step2.name: Connection: Validate before problem-solving
step2.description: This is the hardest part for most parents. You want to fix it, but your teen needs to feel heard first.
what_to_say: "I've noticed you seem down lately. What's going on?"
"You seem really stressed. I'm here to listen."
"I care about you and I want to understand what you're experiencing."
what_NOT_to_say: "Other people have it worse" (comparison, not connection)
"When I was your age..." (makes it about you)
step2.key: Listen 80%, talk 20%. Resist the urge to fix.

step3.name: Labeling: Help them name the emotion
step3.description: Many teens can't articulate feelings. Help them identify what they're experiencing.
examples: "Sounds like you're feeling lonely/overwhelmed/frustrated. Is that it?"
"Help me understand - are you worried about how people see you?"
"This sounds really hard. That makes sense."

step4.name: Problem-solving: Only after connection
step4.description: Now you can offer ideas, but frame it as collaboration.
how: "What do you think might help?" (ask first)
"I have some ideas if you want to hear them"

subsections.title: Opening Conversation Starters
subsections.content:
- "How are you really doing?" (and wait for answer beyond 'fine')
- "What's been the hardest part of this week?"
- "Is there anything I'm missing?"
- "What would help right now?"
Key: Ask open-ended questions, not yes/no.

subsections.title: Reading Non-Verbal Cues
subsections.content:
Teens often won't verbally ask for help. Watch for:
- Withdrawal from activities they loved
- Changes in friend groups or social patterns
- Sleep/appetite shifts
- Academic changes
- Increased irritability or anger
- Neglecting hygiene
- Increased phone/internet use
These are signals your teen needs connection.

content.overview: Each condition responds to different parental supports. Here's what evidence shows works.

conditions.name: Depression
what_helps: Encourage (don't force) gentle movement - even 10-min walk
Normalize low mood while encouraging small activities
Watch for self-harm or suicidal thoughts
Don't take withdrawal personally
Maintain routine (sleep, meals) even if teen resists
what_hurts: Comparing to peers ("Look how happy they are")
conditions.parent_self_care: Depression is exhausting to witness. Take breaks. You can't fill from empty. Seek support.

conditions.name: Anxiety
what_helps: Validate the fear ("I know this feels real to you") but don't reinforce avoidance
Encourage exposure to feared situations gradually ("You're braver than you think")
Teach grounding techniques together (5-4-3-2-1, breathing)
Model calm in your own anxiety
Celebrate courage, not just success
what_hurts: Enabling avoidance (letting them skip school to avoid anxiety)
Expressing your own anxiety (they'll absorb it)
Pushing too hard too fast ("Just do it")
conditions.parent_self_care: Anxious teens have anxious parents often. Work on your own anxiety - they'll mirror your calmness.

conditions.name: Self-Harm
what_helps: Stay calm (your panic makes them defensive)
Listen without judgment first
Understand the function (emotional release? Tangibility of internal pain?)
Help find alternatives (ice cube, drawing on skin, intense exercise)
Professional help is essential - don't try to manage alone
Keep sharp objects in safe place without making it obvious you're restricting
what_hurts: Attempting to be sole support without professional help
conditions.parent_self_care: This is heavy. Get your own therapist. Self-harm is a sign your teen needs professional help NOW.

conditions.name: Social Anxiety
what_helps: Gradual exposure (one social situation at a time)
Celebrate showing up, not social "success"
Practice social scenarios at home (role-play)
Don't force; encourage gently
Help them find small-group activities (easier than large groups)
Validate that social anxiety is real (not 'just shyness')
what_hurts: Forcing participation in large group situations
conditions.parent_self_care: Remember: your anxious teen needs calm, consistent support. You are the stable base.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Seek Professional Help

content.overview: Not every mood dip needs therapy, but these signs warrant professional evaluation.
immediate_crisis: Suicidal statements ("I'd be better off dead", "Everyone would be happier without me")
Sudden calmness after depression (paradoxical recovery can signal plan)
Active self-harm (cutting, burning) with increasing severity
content.call_crisis_line: If any of above: 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or 911
seek_therapist_if: Persistent low mood, anxiety, or emotional dysregulation for 2+ weeks despite normal support
Withdrawal from previously enjoyed activities for 2+ weeks
Sleep or appetite changes lasting weeks
Social isolation or relationship conflicts worsening
Any self-harm behavior, even if mild
Family conflict escalating despite your efforts
Traumatic event (loss, abuse, accident) happened recently
You (parent) are consistently unable to de-escalate conflicts

finding_therapist.step1: Insurance: Call provider, ask for youth mental health providers in your area; most cover therapy
finding_therapist.step2: Credentials: Look for LCSW (Licensed Clinical Social Worker), LPC (Licensed Professional Counselor), PhD/PsyD Psychologist, or MD Psychiatrist
finding_therapist.step3: Modality: Does your teen need CBT? DBT? Trauma-informed? Family therapy?
finding_therapist.step4: Interview: Most therapists offer 15-min initial calls. Ask about their experience with your teen's condition
finding_therapist.step5: First session: Watch for: Does therapist listen to your teen? Do they explain approach? Do they seem to get your family?
finding_therapist.tip: First therapist may not be the right fit. It's okay to try another.

content.overview: Evidence-based things you can do right now to support mental health.

strategies.name: Sleep Environment
strategies.why: Sleep deprivation is the #1 risk factor for depression/anxiety in teens. Adolescents biologically need 8-10 hours. Late phone use delays sleep by 1-2 hours.
what_to_do: Phones out of bedroom by 9pm (at least 1 hour before sleep)
Consistent bedtime/wake time (even weekends)
Dark, cool room (65-68°F optimal)
No screens 30-60 min before bed
Avoid caffeine after 2pm
strategies.how_to_approach: Frame as family rule ('We're all doing this'), not punishment. Your sleep habits matter too - model good sleep.

strategies.name: Physical Activity
strategies.why: Exercise = natural antidepressant. 30 min/day reduces depression by 47%, anxiety by 42% (research).
what_to_do: Find activity they enjoy (not forced sports - could be walks, skateboarding, dancing, YouTube videos)
Start small (10 min) if they're resistant
Do it together sometimes (not all the time)
Celebrate consistency, not performance
strategies.how_to_approach: "Want to go for a walk?" (casual) vs "You need exercise" (resistance invitation). Option is key.

strategies.name: Nutrition
strategies.why: Blood sugar, omega-3s, B vitamins affect mood. Erratic eating worsens anxiety and depression.
what_to_do: Regular meals (skipping breakfast = worse mood)
Protein + complex carbs (stabilizes mood)
Limit sugar/energy drinks (spike then crash)
Model healthy eating (you matter)
strategies.how_to_approach: Not about weight/appearance. Frame as 'food is fuel for your brain.' Invite them to cook together.

strategies.name: Social Connection
strategies.why: Loneliness is 2.5x risk for depression/anxiety. Teens isolate when struggling, but isolation worsens it.
what_to_do: Normalize spending time with friends (don't require it if anxious, but gently encourage)
Create space for teen's friends at home (even if chaotic)
Don't force socializing, but don't allow complete withdrawal
Watch for online-only friendships (can support, but not replace in-person)
strategies.how_to_approach: "I know you're struggling. Research shows connecting with people helps. What if you..." (offer options, not demands)

strategies.name: Limiting Harmful Comparisons
strategies.why: Social media comparison is #1 driver of teen depression/anxiety. Instagram highlights ≠ reality.
what_to_do: Teach critical media literacy ('That's a filtered highlight reel')
Set time limits on social media (not bans - backfire)
Follow positive accounts yourself (model media diet)
Discuss unrealistic standards (Photoshop, surgery, filters)
strategies.how_to_approach: Not anti-technology. Help them use it consciously. "Does this account make you feel better or worse?"

mistakes.why_it_backfires: Invalidates their real experience. Signals you don't understand. They stop sharing.
mistakes.instead: "This is really hard. I'm here. Let's figure this out together."

mistakes.why_it_backfires: Temporarily relieves anxiety, but reinforces that worry is dangerous. Creates dependency on reassurance.
mistakes.instead: First time: answer. After that: "You already know the answer. What would happen if you sat with this worry?"

mistakes.why_it_backfires: Teaches that they can't handle anything. Reduces confidence. Anxiety grows.
mistakes.instead: Support while they face manageable challenges. Encourage gradual exposure.

mistakes.why_it_backfires: Depression/anxiety aren't choices. Punishment teaches shame, not change.
mistakes.instead: Separate behavior from condition. 'I understand you're anxious. I also need you to go to school.' Both can be true.

mistakes.why_it_backfires: Teen feels guilty for causing YOUR stress. Stops opening up.
mistakes.instead: Get your own support. Process with other adults or therapist, not your teen.

mistakes.why_it_backfires: Real suffering gets ignored. Condition worsens. Teen feels unsupported.
mistakes.instead: Take it seriously while maintaining perspective. 'This is hard AND we can get through it.'

mistakes.why_it_backfires: Teen already compares themselves constantly. This amplifies shame.
mistakes.instead: Focus on YOUR teen's experience and growth. 'I'm proud of how you're handling this.'

sections.title: Parent Self-Care: You Can't Pour From Empty

content.overview: Supporting a struggling teen is emotionally draining. Your wellbeing directly impacts their recovery.
content.reality: If you're burned out, anxious, or depressed, your teen will absorb it. Your calm is contagious. Your panic is contagious.

priorities.why: You need your own therapist/support. Not weakness - necessity. Your teen's condition may trigger your own trauma.
Parenting a struggling teen tests relationships. Stay connected to your partner.
priorities.action: Weekly 20-min check-in with partner about how you're each handling it. United front = easier parenting.

priorities.why: Sleep deprivation makes everything worse. Parental worry often kills sleep.
priorities.action: Protect your sleep like you protect your teen's. Even if worried, sleep helps you problem-solve better.

priorities.why: Exercise and nutrition aren't luxuries. They're baseline for managing stress.
Isolation worsens parental stress and depression. You need people outside your family.
priorities.action: One friend date/activity per week that's just for you.

content.permission_to_rest: You don't have to have all the answers. You don't have to 'fix' your teen. You just have to show up, stay calm, and get professional help when needed. That's enough. You're doing better than you think.
